content: Laterality refers to the preference that most humans exhibit for one side of their body over the other. This phenomenon is exemplified by tendencies such as right-handedness or left-footedness. Interestingly, laterality is not exclusive to humans and can also be observed in other animals and even plants. Human Laterality The vast majority of humans are right-handed, and many also demonstrate a general preference for the right side of their body. This includes favoring the right eye, right foot, and right ear when forced to choose between the two sides. The underlying reasons for this preference are not entirely understood, but it is believed to be linked to the dominance of the left cerebral hemisphere of the brain, which controls the right side of the body. The left hemisphere is dominant in most humans, particularly because it serves as the language center in 90–92% of individuals. Human cultures are predominantly right-handed, and this trend may be reinforced both biologically and socially. Linguistic evidence supports this bias. For instance, the English word left originates from the Anglo-Saxon word lyft, meaning weak or useless. Similarly, the French word gauche not only means left but also awkward or tactless. The Latin word sinistra, from which the English word sinister is derived, also means left. Conversely, in many cultures, the word for right often carries connotations of correctness or propriety. The English word right comes from the Anglo-Saxon word riht, meaning straight or correct. Words like adroit and dexterous, which mean skillful, are derived from the French droit and Latin dexter, respectively. This linguistic and social bias is not confined to European cultures. For example, Chinese characters are designed for right-handed individuals, and no significant left-handed culture has been identified globally. When individuals are compelled to use the hand opposite to their natural preference, this is referred to as forced laterality or forced dextrality. Research conducted by the Department of Neurology at Keele University and North Staffordshire Royal Infirmary suggests that forced dextrality may contribute to the observed decrease in the percentage of left-handed individuals in older age groups. Ambidexterity, the ability to use both hands and sides of the body with approximately equal skill, is extremely rare. While a small number of people can competently write with both hands and perform tasks equally well with both sides of their body, even these individuals typically exhibit a preference for one side. However, this preference may vary depending on the activity. For instance, some individuals may write with their right hand but use their left hand for playing racket sports or eating. This phenomenon, known as cross-dominance, may occur in individuals predisposed to left-handedness but trained for right-handedness. The laterality of motor and sensory control has been the focus of recent intensive studies. It has been found that the hemisphere responsible for speech is also the hemisphere of action in general. The command hemisphere is located in either the right or left hemisphere, but never in both. Approximately 80% of people are left-hemispheric for speech, while the remaining 20% are right-hemispheric. Among right-handed individuals, 90% are left-hemispheric for speech, whereas only 50% of left-handed individuals are right-hemispheric for speech; the remainder are left-hemispheric. The reaction time of the neurally dominant side of the body (the side opposite the major hemisphere or command center) is shorter than that of the non-dominant side by an interval equal to the interhemispheric transfer time (IHTT). Consequently, one in five individuals exhibits handedness opposite to their neural wiring, as determined by reaction time studies. Laterality in Other Animals Laterality in animals, also referred to as limb dominance, is a well-documented phenomenon. For example, most racetracks are designed to run counter-clockwise, favoring right-side-dominant horses. These horses take longer strides with their right foreleg, which aids in turning left. Trainers of left-eye-dominant horses may use a blinder on the left eye to encourage the horse to turn its head slightly to the left and mimic the stride pattern of right-side-dominant horses. Parrots often display a preference for one foot when grasping objects, such as fruit during feeding. Studies suggest that most parrots are left-footed. Polar bears, on the other hand, typically use their left paw to kill prey. Evidence of laterality has also been observed in some extinct species, such as mastodons, where fossil remains show differing tusk lengths, indicating a preference for one side.
